findings.title: Unknown Threat Actor Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Target South Korean Finance
findings.summary_md: CrowdStrike Intelligence identified infrastructure from a targeted campaign against South Korean financial organizations that ran from late September to early October 2026 and ended in exfiltrated data. Threat actor controlled open directories contained Claude Code session histories, ARTEX configuration files and Claude memory files, giving researchers a direct view of how the operator used the recently released agentic pentesting tool alongside language models.

findings.title: Hacking on Autopilot: Inside ARTEX Cybercrime Campaigns
findings.summary_md: Check Point found 2,557 systems hosting or having hosted ARTEX panels, including 1,608 live publicly reachable instances, and 10 misconfigured instances exposing the full ARTEX database. The exposed databases showed operator prompts, model choices and agent steps; observed goals were opportunistic financially motivated cybercrime, with agents mostly running autonomously after initial setup. Check Point notes that the developer made the project closed source on October 8 after abuse reports, while forks and backups kept it available.

findings.title: On the hunt for ARTEX: understanding agentic attacks in AWS environments
findings.summary_md: Datadog described ARTEX behavior after initial AWS access from either leaked long-lived access keys or public Cognito sign-ups, with reviewed sessions opening on anonymous S3 reads. In CloudTrail, the most frequent action was FilterLogEvents with a fixed limit of 1000, searching company names combined with Invoice, Billing, Fund and LLC; one observed key was reused from 103.54.154[.]40. The post also documents placeholder probes such as zzz_nonexistent_abc.txt before fuzzing bursts and lists console routes including /tasks and /exploration/intents.

findings.title: ARTEX and AI-Powered Red Teaming Tools: What Defenders Need to Know
findings.summary_md: Unit 42 counted 609 internet-facing ARTEX hosts in October 2026 and 1,323 running CyberStrikeAI, with 21 hosts running both. Its incident response cases turned public password reset pages and exposed APIs into cloud access without a single software vulnerability, using bursts of one to 14 requests about a second apart followed by 25 to 31 second pauses and validating more than 200 client secrets in about three minutes. The report also describes self-correcting retries, canary inputs such as evil[.]com, and a think-then-act cadence consistent with model inference delays.

findings.title: FLASH-20261113-001: Threat Overview of ARTEX Autonomous Penetration Testing Framework
findings.summary_md: FBI FLASH-20261113-001 warned that threat actors use ARTEX to automate intrusions at machine speed from reconnaissance through data exfiltration. The TLP:CLEAR advisory highlights tactics, techniques and procedures plus indicators of compromise, and dates threat actor use of the framework to at least August 2026.

findings.title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
findings.summary_md: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported multiple actors using open source agentic pentest frameworks, including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI, to automate discrete phases of live intrusions. They described patch differential analysis that rapidly weaponizes n-day flaws and an exposed staging server named exploit_agent aimed at French media, entertainment and education websites. Google Security Operations deployed behavioral and volumetric rulepacks for ARTEX, and the report notes that these frameworks trade stealth for speed through recognizable code and forensic artifacts.

findings.title: ARTEX and Its Forks: Agentic Pentest Frameworks as Attack Infrastructure
findings.summary_md: The Cloud Security Alliance research note described ARTEX as a Go-based multi-agent framework with a Next.js console and PostgreSQL store, exposed by default on port 8787. It reported Censys finding 1,465 exposed consoles in early November 2026, 155 of which also hosted other tooling such as Cobalt Strike, Adaptix C2 and CyberStrikeAI, and a trojanized ARTEX Docker image that gave an unauthenticated root shell. The note argues that detection should focus on behavior, identity and control plane telemetry because forks and rebrands defeat file level signatures.

findings.title: Agentic attacks in the wild: Inside three ARTEX investigations
findings.summary_md: Darktrace detailed three ARTEX-related investigations spanning China-nexus espionage, financial sector intrusions and Azure credential collection. It observed BLOODALCHEMY command and control traffic to nginxmysql[.]com and 45.153.126[.]223 between October 23 and November 2, a wisp-agent download from 213.111.150[.]145:8099 on November 5, and credential collection from 43.98.196[.]73 on October 20. The report warns that shared tooling makes ARTEX useful as investigation context but unreliable as an attribution shortcut.

findings.title: Agentic Attacks in the Wild: ARTEX & Offensive AI Frameworks
findings.summary_md: Wiz Research tracked an ARTEX cluster it calls ARTEX-Harvester, tying it at varying confidence to activity at more than a dozen organizations between late October and mid-November 2026, with more than 220 proxy IPs used against a single target. It observed self-labeling artifacts including pentest-recon user agents, pentest workspaces and pods, and incrementing pentest-iNNNNNN task counters. Wiz also reported that ARTEX consoles shipped exposed to the internet by default, often with default credentials, and that leaked operator logs can pair victim telemetry with the attacker planner intents and transcripts.

findings.title: The ARTEX framework
findings.summary_md: F5 Labs traced ARTEX to a GitHub release on July 26, 2026 and the repository removal on October 8 after misuse reports, noting more than 1,000 current repositories and over 1,600 exposed consoles in November 2026. Its analysis lists injection, SSRF, SSTI, leaked credentials and specific RCE CVEs as initial access paths, followed by custom JSP, PHP and ASP web shells, Kerberoasting, forged tokens and exfiltration through residential proxies and TOR. F5 recommends layered WAF, bot and rate limiting controls, API schema enforcement, segmentation and behavioral detection because agent traffic changes from one request to the next.
